subject: Physiology
summary: The preoptic area (POA) of the hypothalamus contains GABAergic neurons that promote sleep by inhibiting arousal centers. Damage or dysfunction can cause insomnia or abnormal thermoregulation.

sections.p: The POA sits in the anterior hypothalamus and integrates temperature, hormonal, and circadian signals to control sleep‑wake cycles and body heat loss.
b: Contains medial and lateral sub‑regions with distinct functions
GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter released by POA sleep neurons

sections.p: GABAergic POA neurons fire during the night, suppressing wake‑promoting nuclei (e.g., tuberomammillary, locus coeruleus). They also activate heat‑loss pathways via vasodilation.
b: Activity rises with melatonin and falls with cortisol
Lesions reduce NREM sleep and raise core temperature

sections.p: Circadian input from the suprachiasmatic nucleus and homeostatic sleep pressure (adenosine) modulate POA firing. Ambient temperature feeds back through skin thermoreceptors.
b: Cold exposure inhibits POA GABA neurons → arousal
Fever shifts set‑point, reducing POA inhibition

sections.p: Disruption of POA GABA output leads to insomnia, hyperthermia, or paradoxical sleep disorders. Infections, trauma, or neurodegeneration can impair this region.
b: Stroke or TB meningitis affecting hypothalamus

sections.p: Understanding POA function helps diagnose central causes of sleep loss and fever of unknown origin, especially in low‑resource settings where imaging is limited.
b: Insomnia with normal polysomnography may suggest central POA dysfunction
Unexplained hyperthermia with intact peripheral sweating points to hypothalamic injury

sections.p: Focus on the link between GABAergic POA neurons, sleep promotion, and thermoregulation. Know how lesions present clinically.
b: POA lesion → reduced NREM, increased core temp

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent high fever (>40 °C) with altered mental status
Acute severe insomnia causing functional impairment
Sudden loss of temperature regulation after head trauma

faq.q: Why does damage to the POA cause fever?
faq.a: Loss of inhibitory GABA signals removes the brake on heat‑production pathways, raising the hypothalamic set‑point.
Benzodiazepines enhance GABA at POA receptors, promoting sleep; antihistamines also increase POA activity indirectly.

faq.q: Is the POA involved in REM sleep?
faq.a: Primarily NREM; REM regulation relies more on the pontine tegmentum, though POA interacts with REM circuits.

exam: Explain how GABAergic neurons in the preoptic area regulate sleep and body temperature.
Describe the clinical signs of a lesion affecting the preoptic area.
List two common causes of central thermoregulatory failure in low‑resource settings.
